segments.say: Now that the day is behind you, let's give the alarm we talked about tonight a gentle partner. Because your body doesn't only have a system for speeding up. It also has a system for slowing down. And one of the simplest ways to invite it in is something you are already doing, right now. Breathing.

You might remember the part of the nervous system that made Jonah's heart race on the platform this morning. It has a quieter sibling, sometimes called the rest and digest system. Where the first one says hurry, this one says, it's alright now. You can rest. You can let your heart slow down.

You don't need to do anything special to find it. For a moment, simply notice your breath as it is. Don't change it yet. Just notice the air coming in, and the air going out. Maybe you can feel it at the tip of your nose. Maybe in your chest. Maybe in the gentle rise and fall of your belly.

There's no right way to breathe here. Some breaths will be short, some long. Some will feel easy, some a little tight. That's fine. Breath is a bit like the tide at the edge of a quiet beach. It comes in, it goes out, and it doesn't need you to manage it.

Now, if it feels comfortable, let the next breath out be a little longer than the breath in. Not forced. Just a little slower, a little softer. As if you were gently blowing on a cup of warm tea, to cool it without spilling a drop.

Let's do that again. Breathe in, easily, through your nose if that's comfortable. And then let the breath out slowly, longer than it came in. Feel your shoulders drop, just a little, as the air leaves. There's nowhere to go. Nothing to finish. Only this slow, warm breath.

Here's the rhythm, if you'd like to follow it. Breathe in, softly. Breathe out, slowly, a little longer. If a small pause comes at the bottom of the breath, let it be there. And then begin again, whenever your body is ready. That's all there is to it.

Some people like to count. In for a few, out for a few more. If counting helps you settle, you can count softly in your mind. If counting makes you feel like you're doing homework, let the numbers go. The breath doesn't need a score. It only needs a little space.

Your mind will probably wander. You might find yourself thinking about something that happened today, or something you need to do tomorrow. That's not a mistake. It's what minds do. When you notice it, simply come back to the breath, the way you would come back to a book after looking up for a moment.

And as your breath grows slower, your heart may follow. Not because you've ordered it to, but because the two are old friends. They have been keeping each other company your whole life. When one of them settles, the other usually listens.

Picture a still lake at dusk. Now and then, a tiny ripple moves across the surface and fades. Each breath out is like one of those ripples. It spreads, slowly, gently, and then the water is calm again. The sky above it is turning soft shades of lavender and gold.

Now let's follow the breath a little further. As you breathe in, imagine the air reaching all the way down into your belly, like warm water filling a bowl. And as you breathe out, imagine it carrying away a little of the day with it.

Let the breath soften your face. Your forehead, which may have been frowning more than you knew. The small muscles around your eyes. Your cheeks. Let them all go loose and heavy, as if you were about to smile but didn't need to.

Let the breath reach your jaw. A lot of us carry the day in our jaw without noticing. Let your teeth part just a little. Let your tongue rest softly. Breathe out, and feel the jaw hang loose and easy, like a gate swinging gently open.

Notice your chest rising and falling. It doesn't need to rise very far. Shallow or deep, quick or slow, it's doing its work, and it has been doing it all day long, even when you weren't paying any attention. Tonight, you can thank it, quietly, for carrying you.

Let your belly be soft. Many of us were taught to hold our stomach in, to sit up straight, to look ready. You don't need to look ready for anything now. Let your belly rise as you breathe in, and fall as you breathe out, like a sleeping cat curled up by a fire.

If words help, you can borrow this gentle phrase. Breathe in calm. Breathe out the day. Not as a command, and not as a test. Just a quiet little sentence to keep the breath company, like a song someone hums while they wash the dishes.

show.text: Breathe in calm, breathe out the day

segments.say: Imagine soft rain falling on a roof above you. Steady and slow, never in a hurry. Each drop arrives in its own time. Your breath can be like that rain. Unhurried. Regular. Belonging to the night, and to no one's timetable.

Somewhere, in our story, Jonah is breathing too. The talk is over. The train is just a memory. He's lying on his back, breathing slowly, and the alarm in his body that rang so loudly this morning has gone quiet. It did its job. Now it's off duty, and so is he.
And so are you. Whatever rang inside you today, whatever made your heart beat faster, it can rest now. The quiet branch is here. The slow breath is here. You don't need to hold on to anything at all.

Keep breathing in your own way, at your own pace. In softly. Out slowly. And if the breath forgets to be slow, that's fine as well. It will find its way. The fire is warm. The room is quiet. And you are allowed to rest.

Notice how much heavier your body feels than it did a few minutes ago. Your arms resting where they are. Your legs resting where they are. Your head held by the pillow, or the cushion, or the back of the chair. Every breath out lets you sink a little further into whatever is holding you, and it holds you without asking anything back.

In a little while, we'll set down the worries of the day, one by one, somewhere safe. But for now, just stay here with the breath. Coming in. Going out. Slower than this morning. Softer than this afternoon. Just right, for tonight.
